passage:
I'm Zeenat, and my little brother Zayan is five. Every night he checks under the bed with a torch, then says, "Go away, go away, zoom zoom," three times, to keep the monsters out. Only then will he let Ammi switch off the light.
Last week his tooth fell out, and he put it under his pillow with a drawing for the tooth fairy. In the morning there was a coin. He told everyone at breakfast the fairy had sparkly shoes.
I don't know how much he believes. But when he forgets the zoom words, he can't sleep. Now our cousin Dilnaz, who's four, says them too.

qa.q: What does Zayan say three times at bedtime?
qa.a: "Go away, go away, zoom zoom."

qa.q: Why can't Zayan sleep when he forgets the zoom words?
qa.a: The words feel like real protection to him, so without them the monsters seem able to come in and he feels unsafe.

qa.q: How could Ammi help if Zayan forgets the words one night?
qa.a: Say them with him calmly, check under the bed together with the torch, and stay a little while until he settles.

qa.q: What might Dilnaz get from copying the zoom words?
qa.a: Dilnaz probably feels braver too, since the older cousin's special words seem to work.

grounding: An older sibling describes a five-year-old brother's bedtime monster checks, protective words and belief in the tooth fairy.

passage:
Monday. Hemant refused to walk past the store cupboard. "A monster lives there. It has long fingers." Omkar, his big brother, opened it to show the brooms. Hemant still ran past.
Wednesday. Hemant tied his lucky red thread around his wrist. "Now the monster can't touch me," he said, and walked past the cupboard very fast, eyes shut.
Saturday. The thread slipped off in the bath. Hemant cried until Omkar found it by the drain. He tied it back on, sighed, and went to play.

qa.q: What did Omkar show inside the store cupboard?
qa.a: The brooms.

qa.q: Why did Hemant still run past after seeing the brooms?
qa.a: Hemant was still scared, because the monster felt real in his imagination, and seeing brooms didn't erase that fear.

qa.q: How could the family support Hemant without mocking the thread?
qa.a: Let him keep the thread, check the cupboard together when he wants, and gently remind him it only holds brooms.

qa.q: What is it like for Omkar to help his brother?
qa.a: Omkar tries hard, showing the brooms and finding the thread, and may feel both patient and puzzled that the fear stays.

grounding: Across a week, a preschool boy fears a cupboard monster and relies on a lucky thread to protect him.

passage:
The storm knocked the power out just after dinner, and the whole flat went black. Mridul, five, dived under the blanket. "The shadow monster comes when it's dark!"
His father, Sumit, lit a candle, but the flame made shapes jump on the wall. Mridul screamed.
Then he pulled out his plastic star wand and waved it at each corner. "Shoo. Shoo. Shoo." He peeked out. "It's gone. The wand works."
Sumit sat beside him and made a rabbit shadow with his hands. Mridul giggled, still gripping the wand.

qa.q: What did Mridul wave at each corner?
qa.a: His plastic star wand.

qa.q: Why did Mridul feel safe after waving the wand?
qa.a: In his mind the wand really chased the monster away, so the corners felt empty and safe again.

qa.q: What did Sumit do that helped during the power cut?
qa.a: He stayed close and turned the scary shadows into a playful rabbit, without arguing about the monster.

qa.q: How might the storm night feel to Sumit?
qa.a: Tricky: the candle he lit made things worse, and he had to find a gentle way to calm his son in the dark.

grounding: During a power cut, a five-year-old boy fears a shadow monster and trusts a toy wand to chase it away.

passage: The stairwell light in their Delhi building clicked off on a timer, and Sahil, five, ran up through the dark shouting, "Zoom-ba-lala! The monster can't catch me when I say it!" His sister Dolma, carrying the milk, said it with him instead of laughing. That night his wobbly tooth came out. He slid it under his pillow. "The tooth fairy comes at twelve exactly," he told Dolma. "She needs the word too." He whispered "Zoom-ba-lala" into the pillow twice, to be safe. In the morning, a shiny coin was waiting.

qa.q: What was Sahil's special word?
qa.a: "Zoom-ba-lala!"

qa.q: Why did Sahil whisper the word into his pillow twice?
qa.a: He believed the word truly protected against the monster and wanted to keep the tooth fairy safe too.

qa.q: How did Dolma handle Sahil's special word, and why did it work well?
qa.a: She said it with him instead of laughing, which helped him feel brave on the stairs without being made fun of.

qa.q: How might Dolma see the dark stairwell, compared with Sahil?
qa.a: Dolma knows it is just a timed light, but she understands that to Sahil the dark feels like it could hold a monster.

grounding: A preschooler uses a special word to protect himself from a monster and believes in the tooth fairy.

passage: "Mummy, you didn't say goodnight to Bunny." "Darshan, I said goodnight to everyone." "Not Bunny. If you miss one, the shadow-man wakes up." "Okay. Goodnight, Bunny." "Now the magic line: shadow-man, shadow-man, sleep till sun." "Shadow-man, shadow-man, sleep till sun." Darshan hugged Bunny to his chest. "Mummy, is he real?" "What do you think, beta?" "A bit real. Only at night." "Shall we look behind the curtain together?" "You look. I'll hold Bunny." Urmila pulled it back. "Just the window and the moon." "Okay. But say the line again, just in case."

qa.q: What was the magic line Darshan asked for?
qa.a: "Shadow-man, shadow-man, sleep till sun."

qa.q: Why does Darshan insist on goodnights to every toy?
qa.a: Darshan is scared that missing even one toy will wake the shadow-man, so saying goodnight to everyone makes him feel safe.

qa.q: What did Urmila do that suited a five-year-old's fears?
qa.a: She played along with the ritual, asked what he thought, and then looked behind the curtain with him to show it was just the window and moon.

qa.q: What is bedtime like for Urmila when Darshan adds a new ritual?
qa.a: It takes longer and she has to be patient, but she stays warm and joins in so he can feel safe enough to sleep.

grounding: A preschooler believes in a shadow-man and uses bedtime rituals and a special line to feel protected.

passage: In their apartment in Vancouver, Jin's front tooth finally came out at dinner. He wrapped it in a tissue and put it under his pillow. "The tooth fairy comes at midnight," he told his friend Tomas on the phone. "She flies in the window." Then he stood by the bed and whispered his special words, "Moon-moon-go-away," three times, to keep the monster under the bed asleep. He checked the window was open a little, for the fairy, and the closet door was shut, for the monster. In the morning a shiny coin was under his pillow. "It worked!" he told Tomas. "The monster stayed asleep and the fairy came!"

qa.q: Where did Jin put his tooth?
qa.a: Under his pillow.

qa.q: Why did Jin say his special words three times?
qa.a: He felt a little scared of the monster under the bed and believed the magic words would keep it asleep and keep him safe.

qa.q: How could Jin's parents respond to his magic words without scaring him?
qa.a: They could enjoy the game with him and gently add that his room is safe, and that he can call them if he feels scared at night.

qa.q: How might Tomas feel hearing the story in the morning?
qa.a: Tomas might feel excited and curious, maybe wanting special words of his own.

grounding: Shows a preschooler believing in the tooth fairy, a monster under the bed and special words that protect him.

passage: At the Pune preschool, Manoj refused to fetch the paint from the store room. "A monster lives in there," he whispered to Devika Miss. "It has green teeth." He had a plan, though. He pressed his thumb to his forehead and said, "Magic shield on!" Then he tiptoed to the door, grabbed the paints, and ran back. "The shield worked." Devika Miss knelt down. "That was brave. Shall we turn the light on and look together?" Manoj held her hand. Inside were brooms, boxes and a mop with a green handle. Manoj pointed at the mop. "Maybe that was it." But he kept his thumb on his forehead, just in case.

qa.q: What did Manoj say the monster had?
qa.a: Green teeth.

qa.q: Why did Manoj press his thumb to his forehead before going in?
qa.a: He was scared of the monster but wanted to be brave, and believed the magic shield would protect him.

qa.q: How did Devika Miss help Manoj without making fun of him?
qa.a: She praised his bravery and offered to look together with the light on, letting him see the room for himself.

qa.q: What would change if Devika Miss had laughed at the monster?
qa.a: Manoj might feel embarrassed and hide his fear next time, and still be scared of the store room.

grounding: Shows a preschooler believing in a monster in the store room and using a special gesture to protect himself.

passage:
Monday: Chinmay heard a scratching noise under his bed. "Monster!" he screamed. Alka Masi came running and turned on the light. Only his toy train, wheels still turning.
Wednesday: Alka Masi and Chinmay made "monster spray" from water and a drop of rose water in an old bottle. Chinmay sprayed under the bed and said, "Go, go, monster, no!"
Friday: Chinmay sprayed, said his words, and got into bed by himself. "Masi, the monster's gone to its own house." He was asleep before the song ended.

qa.q: What made the scratching noise on Monday?
qa.a: His toy train, wheels still turning.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay sleep easily by Friday?
qa.a: He felt safe and brave because he believed the spray and his special words had sent the monster to its own house.

qa.q: Why was the monster spray a kind idea?
qa.a: It gave Chinmay a sense of control over his fear in a playful way, without making fun of him or adding new scary ideas.

qa.q: How might Alka Masi feel on Friday?
qa.a: She likely felt relieved and fond when Chinmay went to bed by himself and fell asleep quickly.

grounding: Shows a preschooler believing in a monster under the bed and trusting special words and a spray to protect him.

passage:
Winter had come, and the power had gone out in the whole village. Bhupen, five, lay in bed in the dark, clutching the blanket.

"Jatin bhaiya, there's a monster under the bed."

His older brother Jatin sighed. "There's no monster."

"There is! I heard it."

Jatin lit a candle and looked under the bed. "See? Only your slippers."

"Say the magic words," Bhupen whispered. "The ones that keep monsters away."

Jatin smiled. "Monster, go home!"

Bhupen let out a breath and snuggled down.

qa.q: What did Jatin find under the bed?
qa.a: Only Bhupen's slippers.

qa.q: Why did Bhupen want Jatin to say the magic words?
qa.a: He felt scared in the dark and believed the special words would protect him.

qa.q: What did Jatin do that helped Bhupen settle?
qa.a: He checked under the bed with a candle to show it was safe, and then played along with the magic words.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel when Bhupen asks for magic words?
qa.a: Jatin seems a little tired but kind, happy to help his brother feel safe.

grounding: A preschooler believes in a monster under the bed and in special words that protect him, as imagination is vivid.

passage:
Holi week had begun in their Jaipur flat. Akash, six, had lost his first tooth. He put it under his pillow very carefully.

"The tooth fairy will come," he told his father Jagdish. "She'll bring a coin. And maybe colours for Holi."

In the morning he found a shiny coin and a tiny packet of pink colour. He ran around the flat shouting, "She came! She came!"

That afternoon, he whispered a special word before stepping into the Holi crowd. "Now nobody can put colour in my eyes."

Jagdish smiled. "And we'll also wear these sunglasses, just in case."

qa.q: What did Akash find under his pillow in the morning?
qa.a: A shiny coin and a tiny packet of pink colour.

qa.q: Why did Akash whisper a special word before the Holi crowd?
qa.a: He felt nervous about colour in his eyes and believed the word would protect him.

qa.q: What did Jagdish do that was wise?
qa.a: He played along with the magic but also gave Akash sunglasses, a real way to protect his eyes.

qa.q: How might Jagdish feel watching Akash shout "She came!"?
qa.a: Jagdish probably feels happy and fond, enjoying Akash's joy and imagination.

grounding: A preschooler believes in the tooth fairy and a special word that protects him, as the line with reality is soft.

passage:
"Sharmila didi, I can't sleep. There's a bhoot in the cupboard."

"A bhoot? On Diwali night?"

"Yes. I saw its eyes."

"Jeevan, those are the diya lights reflecting on the mirror."

"No, eyes!"

Sharmila opened the cupboard. "See, little brother? Clothes. And your red jacket."

"Can you say the special words?"

"Which special words?"

"The ones Nani says."

Sharmila smiled. "Om shanti, bhoot, go home."

Jeevan pulled the blanket up. "Okay. Now it's safe."

qa.q: What did Sharmila say the eyes were?
qa.a: The diya lights reflecting on the mirror.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan ask for the special words?
qa.a: He felt scared of the bhoot and believed Nani's words would keep him safe.

qa.q: What did Sharmila do that helped Jeevan?
qa.a: She opened the cupboard to show only clothes, then said the special words, mixing a real check with gentle play.

qa.q: How might Sharmila feel being asked to say the special words?
qa.a: Sharmila seems amused and caring, happy to help Jeevan feel safe.

grounding: A preschooler believes in a ghost in the cupboard and special protecting words, as imagination is vivid.

passage: Class note, winter week. Raghav told us a monster lives under his bed and only comes out when the heater clicks off. He says "Shoo-shoo-gone!" three times before sleep, and it works, he says. Today he said it before going into the dark store room for crayons. Dilnaz asked if the words would work for her too, and he taught her. Both walked in proudly. I did not tease. I switched on the store room light and said the monster seemed scared of light. I will ask his parents whether bedtime has been hard lately.

qa.q: What does Raghav say three times before sleep?
qa.a: "Shoo-shoo-gone!"

qa.q: How does Raghav feel when he says the words?
qa.a: He feels brave and protected; the words make him feel safe from the monster.

qa.q: What did the teacher get right?
qa.a: Not teasing, playing along gently by switching on the light, and planning to check with his parents whether bedtime has been hard.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel learning the words?
qa.a: She feels included and braver, walking into the store room proudly with Raghav.

grounding: A preschooler believes in a monster under his bed and uses special words to protect himself.

passage: In the summer holidays, Sachin's first tooth fell out while he was eating a guava in the courtyard. He held it up, amazed. "Throw it on the roof!" said his friend Wasim. "Then the sparrow brings a strong new one." Sachin climbed on the charpai and threw hard. The tooth clinked on the tiles. Every morning after that, he felt the gap with his tongue and looked up at the roof. When Aai asked what he was doing, he whispered, "Waiting for the sparrow." Aai smiled. "New teeth take time, sparrow or not."

qa.q: What was Sachin eating when his tooth fell out?
qa.a: A guava.

qa.q: Why did Sachin look up at the roof every morning?
qa.a: He felt hopeful and excited, believing the sparrow would bring his new tooth.

qa.q: How did Aai handle his belief?
qa.a: She smiled and gently said new teeth take time, sparrow or not, without mocking or scaring him.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel when Sachin throws the tooth?
qa.a: Wasim probably feels proud to share the ritual and excited to see whether it works.

grounding: A preschooler believes a sparrow will bring his new tooth after a roof-throwing ritual.

passage: It was the rainy autumn week before Día de Muertos, and Mateo's tooth was finally out. He put it under his pillow in a little paper box. "Ratoncito Pérez will come," he told his big brother Pablo. "But only if I'm asleep. And only if I say goodnight to him three times." He whispered it three times, eyes squeezed shut. In the morning there was a shiny coin and a tiny note. Mateo ran through the house shouting. Pablo winked at Papá. Papá knelt down. "What a lucky morning," he said.

qa.q: Where did Mateo put his tooth?
qa.a: Under his pillow, in a little paper box.

qa.q: Why did Mateo whisper goodnight three times?
qa.a: He believed the special words would make Ratoncito Pérez come, and he felt hopeful and a little nervous about getting it right.

qa.q: What could Papá do if Mateo later asks whether the mouse is real?
qa.a: Answer gently and honestly at Mateo's level, without mocking a belief he enjoyed.

qa.q: How does Pablo see Mateo's excitement?
qa.a: Pablo, who is older, is in on it and enjoys Mateo's joy, winking at Papá.

grounding: A preschooler believes in the tooth mouse and a special goodnight ritual.

passage:
At nap time on a thundery monsoon afternoon, Rafiq wouldn't lie down. He peered under his mat. "There's a monster under here. It comes when it rains."
Lavanya Ma'am crouched beside him. "What does it look like?"
"Green, with wet feet." He whispered, "My magic word makes it run. Zoom-zoom-go!" He said it three times.
He showed the gap in his teeth. "The tooth fairy took my tooth and left a shiny coin. She lives in the fan."
Lavanya Ma'am patted his mat. "Strong word. And I'm right here too." Rafiq lay down, one eye open.

qa.q: Where does Rafiq say the tooth fairy lives?
qa.a: In the fan.

qa.q: Why does Rafiq say his magic word three times?
qa.a: He feels scared of the rain monster, and the special word makes him feel brave and protected.

qa.q: How could Lavanya Ma'am help Rafiq feel safe at nap time?
qa.a: She can respect his magic word, stay close, and later gently explain that thunder is just rain clouds, without mocking him.

qa.q: What would change if Lavanya Ma'am had laughed at the monster?
qa.a: Rafiq might have felt embarrassed and more afraid, and stopped telling her what scares him.

grounding: Shows a preschooler believing in a monster, the tooth fairy and a protective magic word.
